lesson.title: Running the Derivative Backward
lesson.summary: An antiderivative reverses differentiation: given a function that describes a rate of change, an antiderivative recovers a function whose derivative matches it.
lesson.body:
Every operation in mathematics tends to have a mirror image. Addition has subtraction, multiplication has division, and squaring has square roots. Differentiation, the process you already know for turning a function into its rate of change, also has a mirror image. That mirror image is called finding an antiderivative: starting from a derivative and working backward to recover a function it could have come from.

Formally, a function F is called an antiderivative of f on an interval if F'(x) = f(x) for every x in that interval. Notice the direction of the statement carefully. We are not differentiating F to define it; we are looking for an F whose derivative happens to equal a function f that we were already given. This is exactly the skill you built while studying the derivative function: you learned a rule that maps a function to its derivative, and now you are asking that rule to run in reverse.

Here is why this matters beyond being a clever trick. Rates of change are often what we can measure directly. A speedometer reports velocity, not position. A thermometer's reading changes at some rate, but what we often want is the total accumulated change, or the original quantity itself. Antiderivatives are the tool that lets you start from a known rate and reconstruct the quantity that produced it.

Let's work through a concrete example and check it carefully. Suppose f(x) = 3x^2, and we want an antiderivative F. We need a function whose derivative is 3x^2. Recall that differentiating x^3 uses the power rule: bring the exponent down as a multiplier and reduce the exponent by one, giving d/dx[x^3] = 3x^(3-1) = 3x^2. That is exactly f(x). So F(x) = x^3 is an antiderivative of f(x) = 3x^2. You can verify this yourself anytime by differentiating your answer and checking that you land back on the original function.

One more thing to notice before moving on: F(x) = x^3 is not the only function that works. F(x) = x^3 + 5 also has derivative 3x^2, since the derivative of a constant is zero. So a single function f can have many antiderivatives, all differing from one another only by a constant. That observation is the seed of the next idea: collecting all of these antiderivatives into a single, organized expression.
